entry.title: feat: design my lessons — catalogue, tag curation, study plans and th…
entry.content:
feat: design my lessons — catalogue, tag curation, study plans and the tab (#51)

* feat: design my lessons -- catalogue, tag curation, study plans and the tab

Chunks A, B and C of the plan in one change: the material becomes visible, the
learner's intent becomes data, and the tab puts both in front of them.

ADR-0007 covers the part that is a decision rather than a feature.

## The catalogue

`card_state` gains a denormalised `bucket`, written from the single definition in
`core/buckets.py`. Stored rather than recomputed: a threshold that decides policy
must not get a second definition in a WHERE clause, which is the exact shape of
the bug ADR-0002 records. `sync` backfills any state that has none, because a
column added by a migration starts NULL and COALESCE would then report every card
a learner has ever answered as new -- a catalogue confidently wrong about their
own progress.

`store/catalogue.py` is one query and one selector language.
`level=A2,track=gramatica,topic=preposicoes,state=new` is the same string whether
it arrives from the CLI, the web API, or a row in `plan_priorities`; three
parsers for one idea is how they drift. Repeating a dimension widens rather than
contradicts, because two checkboxes mean "either" and contradiction would make an
empty result look like an empty course.

## Curating tags

`repetita tag add|remove|rename|split|merge|list`, all with `--dry-run`. A rename
is course-wide -- a tag renamed on half the material is two tags, which is the
situation this exists to fix rather than to create -- and leaves a `tag_aliases`
row so plans and facets.yaml keep resolving. Every operation marks the notes it
touched as `edited_at`, which is what stops the next import overwriting the change
and makes a genuine clash surface as a conflict.

`repetita export` is owed from ADR-0006 and lands here. The README promises that
adding a lesson is a pull request a non-programmer can make, and once material is
editable in the app that promise depends entirely on writing it back out. It is
also what makes a tag change reviewable: a normal diff on normal files. Note
emission reuses `importers.emit`, so imported and exported material come out in
one format rather than two that drift.

## Plans

Four tables, and `review_log.plan_revision_id`. That column is the reason this is
an ADR: ADR-0003 exists because the predecessor kept aggregates and threw the
sequence away, and "did making it harder actually help?" is the same shape of
question. Adding the link later would work from that day forward and leave every
earlier answer unattributable.

Weights read a priority list as a Zipf curve rather than a linear ramp: over ten
rows linear gives the top 18%, which nobody experiences as "this is what I want
to work on". Allocation is largest-remainder so the budget is spent exactly, and
what a exhausted bucket cannot take flows down the list rather than shrinking the
session -- otherwise a plan would quietly become a cap.

A plan cannot excuse you from review. It decides which *new* material is woven in
and at what share; every owed card is still owed, in the same order.

`policies/` finally gets the `get()`/`names()` registry that `srs/`, `graders/`
and `presenters/` have had all along, plus the `SessionPolicy` protocol
`ARCHITECTURE.md` has listed as an extension point since the beginning.

## Issues

`material_issues` is deliberately not `card_reports`. That table says one
exercise is broken and suspends the card; this says the grouping is wrong and
suspends nothing. Same reasoning that keeps reports out of `review_log`.

## The tab

Drag-to-reorder priorities, three knobs, and a live preview of what tomorrow
would look like. The preview is cheap because the policy is pure, which is what
makes a knob an experiment rather than a commitment.

ADR-0005 governs the new endpoints and is easy to break by accident: card ids are
authored from the material, so a quarter of them are the answer. The catalogue
returns counts and labels only -- never a card id, never a note id, never a note
field -- and a test asserts that over raw response bytes rather than a parsed
field, because a parsed assertion only checks the places you thought to look.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

* fix(store): never stamp a database's schema version backwards

An older build opening a newer database wrote its own `SCHEMA_VERSION` over the
recorded one. The next time the newer build ran, the version it read was lower
than the migration it had already applied, so it replayed it -- "duplicate column
name" on a database that was fine until something read it.

Not theoretical here. The hub serves repetita live from the working tree, so
switching branches over one study database is an ordinary thing to do, and this
change adds the first migration anyone would hit it with.

The stamp now takes the greater of the two.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

---------

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

entry.title: feat(content): read a course's tags as facets (#50)
entry.content:
feat(content): read a course's tags as facets (#50)

`notes.tags` is a JSON array in a TEXT column. It has been written by every sync
since the beginning and read by no query at all, because a JSON blob cannot be
indexed, joined or grouped. Measured across the real course: 676 notes whose
tags mix four different kinds of statement in one namespace -- level (A1/A2/B1),
track (vocabulario/gramatica/musica/fala), topic (tempo/comida/preposicoes) and
provenance (licao-setembro) -- with nothing in the engine able to tell them
apart.

So "the A2 grammar cards about prepositions that are still new" could not be
expressed, let alone counted.

A per-course `facets.yaml` says which question each tag answers, and
`note_facets` is the join table that makes GROUP BY possible.

The tags themselves do not change, and that is deliberate. `importers/hub.py`
records that the predecessor had `track`, `topic` and `level` as three separate
columns and the import flattened them into tags on purpose, because "a tag is
the general form of something true about this note that a course may weight or
filter on". An axis is a reading of that bag, not a replacement for it. No note
file is rewritten by this change.

A note may hold several values on one axis. That is the ordinary case rather
than an edge one: material about ordering food in a market is genuinely both
`comida` and `cidade`, and forcing a choice loses real information. Only `level`
is capped, at one, because two levels would make every count by level disagree
with the total.

One axis may be `catch_all`, which is what makes adding a topic an edit to a
note rather than to a course's configuration. Declared values beat the
catch-all, so promoting a value onto a real axis reclassifies it everywhere with
no note touched.

Taxonomy problems are never fatal. A note filed under nothing is badly filed,
not broken, and quarantining it would take working material away from a learner
over a bookkeeping mistake -- the opposite of what the quarantine is for.

Classification reads the stored notes rather than the incoming files, which
matters under ADR-0006: a note edited here keeps its own tags, and filing the
file's version would put it under something it no longer says.

`facets.yaml` is optional. A course without one gets no axes and no complaints,
so every course written before this is still valid.

`docs/tagging.md` documents the conventions and the loop for changing tags,
written to be actionable by an agent working from an issue -- including the part
that is easy to get wrong in both directions: renaming a tag is safe, because
nothing is keyed on it, unlike an item id.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

entry.title: feat(content): load unit.yaml and the course path (#49)
entry.content:
feat(content): load unit.yaml and the course path (#49)

Three pieces of authored structure reached no query at all.

`unit.yaml` was skipped outright by the loader -- `if path.name == "unit.yaml":
continue` -- so a unit's title and CEFR level were written by the author, sat in
the course directory, and were read by nothing. `Course.path` declares the order
units are meant to be taken in and the prerequisites between them; it was parsed
into a typed model and never looked at. `Course.tag_weights` is documented as
"relative share of each tag when new material is introduced" and had no reader
either.

So: a `Unit` model, a `units` table and a `courses` table, populated by the same
merge that owns the rest of the material.

Ordering comes from `path` where a course declares one. A unit the path does not
mention sorts *after* every unit it does, in directory order, rather than at the
front -- an unlisted unit is material the author has not placed yet, and it
should not jump the sequence they did place.

A missing `unit.yaml` is not a problem. A unit exists because its directory
does; the file only decorates it, and its absence means a unit with no title
yet, which is the normal state of a course being written.

Units are archived rather than deleted, for the same reason notes are:
`notes.unit` joins on this id, and a unit that leaves the files still names the
unit its notes were studied under.

No migration and no version bump. `courses` and `units` are wholly new tables,
and `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` in `SCHEMA` reaches an existing database on the
next connect -- which is exactly the case the contract beside `MIGRATIONS` says
needs no step.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

entry.title: feat(store): the database owns the material (#48)
entry.content:
feat(store): the database owns the material (#48)

ADR-0006. `courses/*.yaml` becomes an import/export format; `notes` and `cards`
stop being a cache that is wiped and re-derived on every load.

`sync()` merges instead of replacing. Four outcomes per note: inserted when it
is new, left alone when the source is unchanged, updated when the source
changed, and -- the one the design turns on -- a reported *conflict* when a note
was edited here and changed at the source. The local note stays and the id comes
back in the report. Choosing a winner automatically is the only behaviour that
would make an import unsafe to run, because the loser is unrecoverable and
nothing in the UI would say so.

A note that has left the files is archived, never deleted. Deleting would orphan
`card_state` rows whose history cannot be reconstructed from anything. That is
also why this schema still has no foreign keys: ownership makes the old
reasoning stronger, not weaker, since a note removed in the app must never
cascade into someone's schedule.

The property that used to be free is now maintained on purpose. "A card whose
note vanishes keeps its history" held because nothing linked the tables -- a
property of the *absence* of a mechanism. Archiving replaces that absence with a
mechanism, so the guarantee is re-pinned rather than inherited: a removed note's
row survives, its `card_state` survives, material that comes back returns on the
schedule it left with, and no sequence of imports changes `review_log`.

Archived rows must be excluded by every content query or archived material stays
in circulation. Two needed it: the session queue and `card_ids()`.
`lesson_first_seen_on` deliberately does not -- it counts answers that really
were given, and an answer is not retracted by its note leaving the course.

`content_hash` covers the note as authored and excludes `origin`: moving a note
to another file is not a change to the material, and hashing the path would turn
any reorganisation of a course into a wall of conflicts.

`sync()` now returns a `SyncReport` rather than a bare pair of counts. A merge
that cannot report a conflict is a merge that hides one.

Export is owed next. The README promises that adding a lesson is a pull request
a non-programmer can make, and once material can be edited here that promise
depends on writing it back out.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

entry.title: fix(store): export recent_ratings_for from the package facade (#47)
entry.content:
fix(store): export recent_ratings_for from the package facade (#47)

`__all__` has listed `recent_ratings_for` since the function was written, but
the `from .reviews import (...)` block never imported it. `from repetita.store
import *` therefore raised AttributeError, and `store.recent_ratings_for` did
not exist.

Nothing noticed because nothing in this repo uses a star import, and every
internal caller reaches through the module object for names that *are* imported.
`__all__` is a promise made to code outside the repo, and it was being broken
silently.

The test guards the whole facade rather than this one name: every entry in
`__all__` must resolve on the module. A flat re-export surface makes this
mistake easy to repeat -- each new module under `store/` means another import
block and another set of `__all__` entries to keep in step -- and the next
occurrence should fail in CI rather than in someone's editor.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

entry.title: fix(store): stamp a fresh database without replaying migrations (#45)
entry.content:
fix(store): stamp a fresh database without replaying migrations (#45)

* fix(store): stamp a fresh database without replaying migrations

`_apply_schema` runs `SCHEMA` first, then reads `schema_version` from `meta`
to decide which steps in `MIGRATIONS` still need applying. On a database that
did not exist a moment ago there is no `meta` row, so `current` was 0 and every
step was replayed -- against tables `SCHEMA` had just created in their final
shape.

`MIGRATIONS` is empty and has never had an entry, so nothing has hit this. But
the first real `ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN` anyone appends would fail with
"duplicate column name", and only on newly created databases: green on the
machine of whoever wrote it, red on a fresh clone and in CI. That is a poor
thing to leave for the next person to find.

Ask whether the database is empty *before* `SCHEMA` runs -- afterwards a new
database is indistinguishable from a fully migrated one -- and treat a fresh one
as already at `SCHEMA_VERSION`. An *existing* database with no `meta` row is a
different case, predating versioning, and correctly still starts at 0.

The contract this depends on is now written next to `MIGRATIONS`: `SCHEMA` is
always the cumulative result of applying every step to an empty database.

Tests use a toy schema rather than the real one, so they pin the mechanism
rather than whatever `SCHEMA` happens to contain, and cover all four routes:
fresh, upgraded, both-reach-the-same-shape, and reconnect-does-not-rerun.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

* fix(store): run migrations before the schema on an existing database

A second ordering bug in the same mechanism, found by adding the first real
migration to this repo -- an ALTER that adds a column, plus an index on it,
which is the ordinary shape of a migration rather than an exotic one.

`SCHEMA` describes the tables as they are *now*, so it names the new column.
Executing it before the migrations meant creating an index over a column an
existing database does not have yet:

    sqlite3.OperationalError: no such column: colour

on precisely the databases the migration exists for, and on no fresh one. Same
failure mode as the bug in the previous commit, from the opposite direction:
there, a fresh database replayed steps it did not need; here, an existing one
ran the end state before the steps that produce it.

So the two paths are now separate and each does only what it should. A fresh
database runs `SCHEMA` and nothing else. An existing one runs the migrations it
still owes and then `SCHEMA`, which is idempotent and picks up any wholly new
table. `meta` is created explicitly before the version is read, because a
database old enough to predate versioning does not have that table at all and
the read would fail.

The contract next to `MIGRATIONS` now says what a step may assume: tables that
already exist, and columns it has itself just added -- but not a table
introduced in the same version, which `SCHEMA` creates afterwards.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

---------

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

entry.title: feat(web): offer "I know this" after a correct answer too (#46)
entry.content:
feat(web): offer "I know this" after a correct answer too (#46)

The control only existed on the question. But getting a card right is often the
moment you realise you never needed to be asked -- and until now the only way to
act on that was to keep answering it correctly for months until it retired
itself.

Offered only after a pass. Declaring "I know this" straight after a miss
contradicts the evidence just recorded, and would turn the button into a way out
of a card you have demonstrably not learnt. A near-miss still gets the offer:
HARD is a pass (ADR-0002), so a missing accent does not cost it -- the same line
the grader already draws.

"Next" stays first in the row and keeps focus, so Enter still advances and the
control that retires a card stays something you aim at deliberately. That is the
same reasoning that kept a keyboard shortcut off it.

No server change: `declare_known` retires by `replace`, so the interval the
answer just earned survives, and `undo_known` puts the card back exactly as it
was. Undo does not re-queue the card in this case -- it has already been graded
and scheduled, and putting it back would collect a second answer for one
meeting, which is what sibling burying exists to prevent.

Tests pin the invariants the new offer depends on, since none of them were
covered for an already-answered card: the answer stays in the review log, the
schedule it earned is kept, the retirement is still `declared` rather than
`earned` even though evidence now exists, and undo returns the card to its
answered state.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

entry.title: feat(web): report a broken exercise from inside the session (#44)
entry.content:
feat(web): report a broken exercise from inside the session (#44)

* feat(store,web): report a broken exercise, and take it out of the queue

Studying turns up content bugs no validator can catch. `validate` finds the
structural faults -- an exercise containing its own answer, a choice with too few
options -- but not the ones that only appear under a real answer: a gap that
accepts a word the `answers:` list does not, a cue that does not narrow, a
translation that is simply wrong. Those were discovered mid-session and then
lost, because the moment of discovery is a study session and the moment of repair
is a terminal.

A report is a third kind of thing, next to answering and declaring known.
Answering is evidence about a memory; declaring is a claim about a memory; this
is a claim about the *material*, and the only one of the three that someone has
to go and edit a file about. So:

* it writes nothing to `review_log` -- a report is not an answer, and letting it
  in would corrupt every accuracy figure computed from there, including the gate
  that decides how fast new material arrives;
* it lives in its own table rather than in the content cache, which is wiped and
  re-derived from the very files the report is complaining about;
* it snapshots the note as authored, because the next load rebuilds `notes` --
  and the load that follows someone reading the report is the one that destroys
  the evidence for it.

The card is suspended, not retired. Those are separate lanes in `is_active` and
they mean opposite things: retired is "done with this", suspended is "not now".
Setting `suspended_at` needs no scheduler changes at all -- `is_due` covers due
work, and `introduction_order` and the consolidation branch both filter on
`is_active`, so a card reported on its first showing does not come back tomorrow.

`card_reports.suspended` records whether *this* report is what took the card out.
Without it, undoing a report on a card the importer had already parked would
resurrect material someone deliberately put away.

Reasons are codes rather than prose, and each one names the key an author would
edit -- `also_correct` appends to `answers:`, `ambiguous` sharpens `cue:` -- which
is what makes triage mechanical instead of interpretive. An unknown reason is
refused rather than folded into `other`: a report nobody can act on is worse than
no report, because it looks like one.

The table arrives via `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` in `SCHEMA`, which reaches new
and existing databases alike. Deliberately no `MIGRATIONS` entry and no
`SCHEMA_VERSION` bump: the list gates nothing while it is empty, and bumping the
version would stamp every database as migrated when nothing ran, silently
skipping the first real migration someone writes later.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

* feat(web,cli): a control to report an exercise, and a way to read the reports

The control sits in the aside row beside "I know this", understated for the same
reason and with no keyboard shortcut for the same reason -- it takes a card out
of rotation, and unlike "I know this" it also makes work for someone.

It appears twice, and the second place is the one that matters. Before answering,
a learner can say the question is ambiguous or the translation is wrong. Only
after the verdict can they say the expected answer is wrong, or that what they
typed was right too -- until then they have not been shown the answer to disagree
with. Both of those are the reports most worth having, so `verdict()` now takes
the card in order to offer them.

Opening the picker does not post. One tap to open and one to send costs a tap and
buys not keeping six buttons permanently beside an open question. The optional
note rides along with whichever reason is tapped, so the common case stays two
taps and the rare case needs no second write.

Undo differs between the two moments and the difference is easy to miss: from an
open question the card goes back to the front of the queue, but after a verdict
it has already been answered and pushing it back would re-ask it in the same
session -- which is what `bury_siblings` exists to prevent.

Reports are deliberately not queued offline. `flushPending` replays answers only,
and a report replayed twice is two rows in a work queue; telling the learner it
needs a connection is honester than dropping it quietly.

`repetita reports` is the other half. Without it the reports are write-only, and
a queue nobody can read is a queue nobody empties. It prints the reason, the
snapshot as it read when reported, what the learner typed, and the file and line
to go and edit -- probing `units/<unit>/notes/<origin>` then `units/<unit>/
<origin>`, in the loader's own precedence order, because `Note.origin` is a bare
filename and resolving in the other order would name a file the loader ignored.
The line comes from a textual scan rather than a parser: `yaml.safe_load` throws
line numbers away, and a loader that kept them would be a second implementation
of what a note is.

`test_forms.py` gains the same cross-check it already makes for forms, one layer
up: a reason the client offers that the server refuses is a 400 the learner
cannot act on, and a reason the server takes with no label renders an `undefined`
button. Each side is internally consistent in both cases, so only a test that
reads both can see it.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

---------

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

entry.title: fix(web): tell the client where the app is mounted (#43)
entry.content:
fix(web): tell the client where the app is mounted (#43)

Every call went to a root-relative path. Standalone that is correct; mounted
under a host prefix it 404s on the first request, which is exactly what happened
the first time repetita was registered in hub -- statics resolved, the page
rendered, and the session never loaded.

The server is the only thing that knows the prefix, so it says it:
`<body data-base="{{ url_for('repetita.index') }}">`, and `api.js` prefixes every
path with it. Standalone that is "/" and nothing changes.

Tested in both arrangements, including that `/api/state` is a 404 on the host --
if it ever answered, the base would stop mattering and this would come back
without anything noticing.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

entry.title: feat(web): mount repetita on an application someone else owns (#42)
entry.content:
feat(web): mount repetita on an application someone else owns (#42)

`init_app(app, course_dir, url_prefix=...)` registers the blueprint on a host's
Flask object. Everything the blueprint needs is already read through
`current_app`, so a host only has to supply it; the four lines `create_app` used
to do around `register_blueprint` are now shared rather than duplicated, because
two versions would drift and the thing they would drift about is which material
is served.

The point of mounting is what the host brings. Repetita has no authentication of
its own -- inside a host with a `before_request` gate it does not need any, and
that is tested rather than assumed.

`index.html` includes `repetita_chrome.html` if the host ships one, and nothing
if it does not. That is the whole navigation contract: a host puts its own tab
bar above the app, and standalone the page is complete on its own. Neither
arrangement is the special case.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

entry.title: feat(web): reload course content without a restart (#41)
entry.content:
feat(web): reload course content without a restart (#41)

Adds POST /api/reload and the repetita-licao skill. Committed before the history

entry.title: feat(web): "I know this" — take a card out of the queue on the learne…
entry.content:
feat(web): "I know this" — take a card out of the queue on the learner's word (#40)

One button, not the four the predecessor had. It says "I already know this" and
takes the card out of rotation.

Recorded as `declared`, never as `earned`. Both land a card in the same place and
mean opposite things -- one is months of correct answers, the other is one click
-- and keeping them apart is what makes the claim checkable later instead of
indistinguishable from evidence. Declaring will not relabel an earned
retirement, and undo will not reverse one: putting evidence back needs the same
evidence that took it out, which belongs to a review flow rather than to a
button.

It writes nothing to the review log. Declaring is not an answer, and letting it
in would corrupt every accuracy figure computed from that log -- including the
gate that decides how fast new material arrives.

A card never answered has no state row, and that turned out to be the commonest
case for this button: meeting a new card and already knowing the word. A test
caught it; the fix is in the code, not the test.

Undo costs the card nothing -- no interval, no lapse. "Actually, I don't know
it" is not the same as getting it wrong.

No keyboard shortcut. The predecessor had one and removed it after a stray
keystroke retired an item, and the button is styled quiet for the same reason:
a control that takes a card out of rotation should not sit where a thumb lands
on the way to answering.

Also removes `card_id` from the answer payload -- the last place an id still
left the server -- and brings the changelog up to date with this phase.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

entry.title: feat(web): keep answers given offline, and persist handles so they su…
entry.content:
feat(web): keep answers given offline, and persist handles so they survive (#39)

An answer given without a connection was lost: the `catch` in `submit()` wrote a
status line and nothing else. Answers now go to localStorage and are sent when
the connection returns.

The queue follows the shape the predecessor arrived at the hard way: claim and
clear the whole queue up front, retry only network failures, and merge anything
added mid-flight in a `finally`. Leaving items in place while sending them is how
one gets sent twice, when an `online` event fires a second flush over the same
rows.

That required changing a decision. Handles were minted per run (ADR-0005), which
was fine while a restart only meant "refetch the session" -- but an answer queued
offline and posted after a restart would have resolved to nothing and been lost,
which is the exact failure the queue exists to prevent. Handles are now persisted
in `card_handles`. Nothing in the guarantee depended on regeneration: a token is
random and says nothing about the material whether it lives an hour or a year,
and the threat model is a learner reading the DOM. ADR-0005 amended rather than
replaced, so the reasoning stays visible.

The distinction between an unreachable server and a server that said no is
load-bearing and is now made once, in `api.js`: offline keeps the answer, a
refusal drops it and says so. An answer disappearing without a word is the thing
this module exists against, so even the dropped ones are counted.

Verified in a browser, not by unit test alone: two answers given with the network
cut show "2 answers saved here", come back as "2 sent", and land in review_log
(462 -> 464). Then the case the handle change was for -- answer offline, restart
the server, reconnect: "1 sent", and the row is there.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

entry.title: fix(store): retire a card that has earned it, and move the rule out o…
entry.content:
fix(store): retire a card that has earned it, and move the rule out of the scheduler (#38)

`sm2.should_retire()` and `is_leech()` existed, had unit tests, and **nothing
called them**. `record_answer` only carried `retired_at` forward, so no card
would ever have left the queue -- after months of study everything would still be
in rotation. The unit tests passed throughout, which is what made it invisible.

The plan said to add `should_retire` to `SchedulerBackend`. That is the wrong
layer. Retirement is policy over what the store already records -- the interval,
the lapse count, the recent ratings -- not a property of a memory model. Putting
it on the protocol forces Leitner and FSRS to hold an opinion neither has: FSRS's
own position is that nothing is ever finished, it just schedules further out, and
Leitner has no notion of a clean run at all.

So both rules moved to `core/retirement.py`: pure functions over plain values,
reachable from `store` without importing `policies` and inverting the layering.
A clean run is read from the review log rather than from SM-2's `reps`, because
every backend writes the same log and only one of them keeps that counter.

Measured on the real path: a card retires after ten clean answers at a 90-day
interval, reason `earned`. A declared retirement is not relabelled as evidence by
a later answer, and retirement survives a content reload.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

entry.title: fix(web): render the choice form, and test that the two sides agree (…
entry.content:
fix(web): render the choice form, and test that the two sides agree (#37)

`choice` was added to `SUPPORTED_FORMS`, the serialiser started shipping
shuffled `options`, and no client module was ever written for it. The client hit
`MODES[card.form] === undefined` and **silently skipped the card** -- a status
line, not an error, with valid JSON on the wire. Measured on the real corpus:
546 of 676 cards at first contact.

I verified that change with curl against the API and never opened a browser,
which is exactly the class of failure a browser would have shown in one look.

The renderer itself is small: options arrive already shuffled and already
filtered (a choice is refused outright unless real distractors exist), so this
module only draws them and must not reorder. Picking disables the row, since a
double tap would otherwise post a second answer for a card already being graded.

The test is the point. `tests/web/test_api.py` asserted that a served form is in
`SUPPORTED_FORMS` and passed, because the gap was *between* the server's list and
the client's. `tests/web/test_forms.py` reads both and compares them, in both
directions, plus a shape check that a form module talks to `submit()` and never
to the network -- grading is server-side, and a module with `fetch` could route
around that. Parsing JavaScript from a Python test is ugly and is the only place
these two worlds meet without a browser.

Verified by unregistering `choice` and watching the new test fail, then in a real
headless browser: 3 choice cards drawn out of 12, zero skipped, no console
errors.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

entry.title: docs: make room for NonCommercial source material, outside git (#36)
entry.content:
docs: make room for NonCommercial source material, outside git (#36)

The open textbook the first course follows turns out to be CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, not
plain CC as THIRD-PARTY.md claimed. The NC clause is one-way incompatible with
the CC BY-SA course content: BY-SA permits commercial use and NC forbids it, so
no amount of transformation relicenses it.

That does not make the book useless -- reading a textbook and then writing your
own exercises is what a textbook is for. It means the extracted material has to
live on one side of a line a later contributor cannot cross by accident.

So `reference/` exists, with everything under it gitignored, and its README says
plainly that the reason is the licence and not the file size -- because the
extract is a few hundred kilobytes, and "it's small, let's just commit it" is
exactly the thought that would undo this.

Corrects the THIRD-PARTY row: structure only. Which grammar point precedes which
is a fact about teaching a language and following it is fine; the sentences,
tables and passages are not ours to ship.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

entry.title: feat(content): rank distractors by shared stem and by how common a wo…
entry.content:
feat(content): rank distractors by shared stem and by how common a word is (#34)

Closes the paradigm and frequency half of the distractor work.

`morphology` -- a candidate sharing a stem with the answer -- is the hardest
kind of option to eliminate without knowing the grammar, because for a Romance
language it IS the conjugation paradigm. On the real corpus it produces exactly
the sets the exercise is testing: `passada` against `passado`, `ainda` against
`ainda assim`, `saio` against `saem` and `saímos`. 570 of 3360 distractors now
come from it.

It carries two thresholds and both are load-bearing. A short answer has no stem
to share: `o` and `ontem` agree on one letter by coincidence, and honouring that
ranked `ontem`, `outubro` and `onze` above `as` as options for an article --
measurably worse than no signal. A long answer needs only two characters, since
`sa|io` against `sa|em` is a real paradigm. A length floor separates the two
cases; a bare count of shared characters cannot, and my first attempt at one
made the article cards worse.

Frequency ranking uses `wordfreq` behind an optional extra. Its absence changes
the order of options within a tier, never which are eligible or how they are
labelled, so a course built with it and one built without differ in polish
rather than correctness. The language comes from `course.l2.code`; the engine
holds no language knowledge of its own.

`mlconjug3` was the planned source for paradigms and is not usable: it fails to
import under scikit-learn 1.9 (`No module named '_loss'`, its pickled models
predate the move) and pulls 232MB for the privilege. Recorded in THIRD-PARTY.md
so the next person does not spend the afternoon I did.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

entry.title: feat(content): precomputed distractors, and serving the choice form (…
entry.content:
feat(content): precomputed distractors, and serving the choice form (#33)

Closes #32.

Multiple choice was refused outright because there was nothing honest to put
beside the answer. There is now: a `distractors` table, computed at content sync
from two sources -- the note's own `distractors:` field, which is the author
saying "this is the mistake I expect" and beats any heuristic, and other notes'
answers to the same field of the same note type, nearest in length, from the
same unit before the wider course.

This is a scheduling concern, not a rendering one. Options that can be
eliminated without knowing anything mean the card is answered correctly whatever
the learner knows, which inflates measured accuracy -- and accuracy is what
opens the new-material gate. A multiple choice with filler options would make
the app introduce material faster than anyone can absorb it. So `choice` is
capability-gated on having real distractors and is simply not offered otherwise,
and `validate` reports the cards that lose the form so the author knows.

Generation is deterministic. Anything random would churn the table on every
content rebuild and make a content diff unreadable; the shuffle happens when the
card is served.

On the real corpus: 560 of 676 cards resolve a full set, and a session now
serves choice, typein, wordbank and flashcard rather than typein alone.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

entry.title: fix(import): never overwrite a card answered in this engine (#31)
entry.content:
fix(import): never overwrite a card answered in this engine (#31)

Re-importing overwrote every `card_state` row unconditionally. That was harmless
while the predecessor was the only place studying happened and this database was
a reproducible copy of it. It stops being harmless the moment anyone answers a
card here: the import would silently revert a real answer to the state it was
imported in, which is the same failure the append-only review log exists to
prevent, arriving through a different door.

Imported history is stamped `sm2-legacy`, so any other algo in the log is an
answer given here. Those cards keep their state and are reported; everything
else still refreshes. A dry run says what it would keep without writing, since
that is the number worth seeing before running it for real.

Proven on the running instance, not only in tests: a card answered twice here
went from seen 3 to 5, a full re-import from the predecessor left it at 5, and
two card states were reported as kept.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

entry.title: fix(policies): hold a note's siblings back from today, do not requeue…
entry.content:
fix(policies): hold a note's siblings back from today, do not requeue them (#29)

* fix(policies): hold a note's siblings back from today, do not requeue them

Closes #27.

`bury_siblings` moved a note's extra cards to the end of the queue. That reads
as burying and is not: the whole queue ships in one `/api/session` batch, so
both siblings reached the learner in the same sitting anyway -- the exact thing
ADR-0001 requires this to prevent, since the second card is then answered from
the first rather than from memory.

Held back now means not served today. The card keeps its due date, unpenalised,
and comes up in the next session; over three days a three-card note is seen
three times, once each. That is Anki's semantics for the same reason.

The count is reported on `/api/session` rather than left silent: a queue shorter
than the stated debt deserves a visible cause.

No effect on the imported corpus, where every legacy type maps to a single-
template note type and no note has siblings. It bites the moment content uses
`vocab` or `picture`, which is what the sample course already does -- serving 7
cards from 4 notes before this, 4 after.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

* test(web): drive the session until the plan is exhausted, not twice

The end-to-end session test assumed two passes covered every card. That held
while one note meant one card. Holding siblings back to a later session makes
the number vary -- a two-card note needs a further round before its second card
is introduced at all -- so the test now runs until the queue is empty or turns
to consolidation, and asserts every card was reached.

Caught by CI, not locally: the failure only appears once the branch is merged
with a main that already has the presentation ladder.
